questions.question: Lena's first paycheck is for $400, but only $337 lands in her bank. Who took the missing $63 before she ever saw it?
questions.answer: FICA, payroll tax for Social Security and Medicare
choices: FICA, payroll tax for Social Security and Medicare
Her bank, a one-time account opening fee
The store, a deposit on her work uniform
Her boss, rounding her hours down by error
questions.context: FICA takes 7.65% of every paycheck: 6.2% Social Security plus 1.45% Medicare. On $400 that is $30.60; the rest is income-tax withholding. The teen never sees the gross.

questions.question: Lena's $400 paycheck cost her boss $463. She saw the $63 taken from her stub. What about the OTHER $63?
questions.answer: The employer half of FICA, Lena's hidden wage
choices: The employer half of FICA, Lena's hidden wage
A bonus the boss kept for hiring a new worker
Cash sent to the store's general repair fund
The cost of training her on the cash register
questions.context: Employers must match FICA dollar-for-dollar: 7.65% from the worker, 7.65% from the employer. Economists call the combined 15.3% the tax wedge: money that would otherwise be Lena's wage. She sees half; the other half is unseen.

questions.question: Jake's uncle says, 'Don't take the raise, the next bracket will eat it.' Is the uncle right?
questions.answer: No, only dollars above the bracket line get the higher rate
choices: No, only dollars above the bracket line get the higher rate
Yes, the whole salary gets taxed at the new rate
Yes, but only in the first year after the raise
Maybe, it depends on the state you live in
questions.context: US tax brackets are marginal, not average. If the bracket jumps from 12% to 22% at $47,150, a $1,000 raise above the line is taxed at 22%, so the worker keeps $780. A raise always leaves you with more money.

questions.question: Maya sold at 11 months for a $1,000 gain. Her friend sold the same stock at 13 months. Why did Maya owe more tax?
questions.answer: Short-term gains (under 1 year) hit ordinary rates
choices: Short-term gains (under 1 year) hit ordinary rates
Maya forgot to file her capital gains form
Her friend used a broker with cheaper fees
Maya's stock was traded on a foreign exchange
questions.context: Hold a stock 1 year and 1 day, and the gain qualifies for long-term rates (0%, 15%, or 20%). Sell at day 364 and you pay ordinary rates, often 22% or 24%. The tax code pays you to hold.

questions.question: Ben, 16, earns $3,000 and owes $0 tax. Dad says 'Roth, not Traditional.' Why?
questions.answer: Roth locks tax-free growth; the Traditional break is worth $0
choices: Roth locks tax-free growth; the Traditional break is worth $0
Roth IRAs guarantee higher returns than Traditional
Teens are legally required to use Roth accounts only
Traditional IRAs charge much higher annual fees
questions.context: Traditional IRA gives a deduction NOW. At 0% bracket that deduction is worthless. Roth dollars come out tax-free at retirement. A teen Roth can grow for 50+ years untouched by the IRS.

questions.question: Sam's job adds $1 to his 401(k) for every $1 he saves, up to 5% of pay. Sam saves $0. What's missed?
questions.answer: Free money, a 100% return before any market gain
choices: Free money, a 100% return before any market gain
A small tax deduction worth a few dollars yearly
Access to a savings account he could use anytime
A free company T-shirt given out at year-end
questions.context: An employer match is one of the few guaranteed 100% returns in finance. Workers who skip the match leave thousands per year, and hundreds of thousands over a career. The 5% you skip is wage the company already budgeted.

questions.question: Olivia owes $3,000 at 24% APR. The minimum payment is $60. Paying only $60 monthly, how long until paid off?
questions.answer: Over 30 years, interest eats nearly every payment
choices: Over 30 years, interest eats nearly every payment
About 50 months, almost exactly four years
About 1 year, the minimum clears it quickly
Forever, there is no way to ever pay it off
questions.context: On a $3,000 balance at 24%, monthly interest alone is about $60. The minimum payment keeps the principal stuck while the card collects interest indefinitely. Credit-card APRs of 22-29% are wealth destroyers.

questions.question: Dad wires $5,000 to a scammer. The bank says it's gone. What could ACH have done?
questions.answer: ACH payments can be reversed if proven fraudulent
choices: ACH payments can be reversed if proven fraudulent
ACH and wire transfers work in exactly the same way
Banks always reverse wires when the sender asks them
Banks by law must refund every scam payment quickly
questions.context: Wires settle same-day and are final. Fees of $25-50 reflect that. ACH transfers take 1-3 business days and CAN be reversed within 60 days for fraud. Scammers always demand wires. Irreversibility costs money.

questions.question: Anna earns $40,000 W-2. Her boss spent $43,060 hiring her: the extra $3,060 was the employer's FICA. Another $3,060 came off Anna's stub. The 15.3% combined bite is called the 'tax wedge.' What does the name reveal?
questions.answer: The wedge between what the boss pays out and what the worker takes home
choices: The wedge between what the boss pays out and what the worker takes home
The triangular shape brackets form when graphed against salary
The split between Social Security and Medicare inside FICA
The gap between federal spending and the revenue available
questions.context: The tax wedge is Bastiat's seen-vs-unseen at the labor-market level. The worker sees only her half; the employer half is also her wage. The Tax Foundation puts the total US labor tax wedge near 30% once income tax is added.

questions.question: Before 2017, about a third of US filers itemized. After Trump's TCJA roughly doubled the standard deduction to $12,000 single / $24,000 married, only ~10% itemized. What changed?
questions.answer: Itemizing now only beats standard with a mortgage AND high state-and-local taxes
choices: Itemizing now only beats standard with a mortgage AND high state-and-local taxes
Itemizing was eliminated by law, only the standard deduction remains for filers
Itemizing got easier, the IRS dropped rules on which deductions filers may claim
Itemizing now requires a tax attorney, the forms became too complex for filers
questions.context: TCJA also capped the State And Local Tax (SALT) deduction at $10,000, squeezing high-tax-state itemizers. Most US taxpayers now take the standard deduction.

questions.question: A Lyft driver gets a 1099-NEC instead of a W-2. She owes the full 15.3% self-employment tax, but deducts gas and mileage her W-2 friend can't. The trade-off?
questions.answer: 1099 pays both FICA halves and deducts business costs; W-2 splits FICA and loses those write-offs
choices: 1099 pays both FICA halves and deducts business costs; W-2 splits FICA and loses those write-offs
1099 pays no payroll tax but gets no Social Security or Medicare ever
1099 and W-2 pay identical taxes; only the paper form they get differs
1099 pays double income tax but the same FICA as a W-2 worker
questions.context: Self-employment tax (Schedule SE) hits both halves of FICA because a sole proprietor IS both. Schedule C lets her deduct gas, mileage, phone, supplies, costs invisible to a W-2 worker. The classification is structural.

questions.question: Warren Buffett said his favorite holding period is 'forever.' In 2011 he told the Senate he paid a lower rate than his secretary. How does the long-term capital gains rate (max 20%) compare to her ordinary income rate?
questions.answer: Lower, the code rewards holding stocks over earning wages
choices: Lower, the code rewards holding stocks over earning wages
Higher, gains are taxed at the top rate plus a surcharge
Identical, gains and wages have matched since 1986
Variable, gains rates change weekly with the S&P 500
questions.context: Long-term capital gains rates are 0% / 15% / 20% depending on income. The top ordinary bracket is 37%. Buffett's complaint became the 'Buffett Rule' debate. The incentive is real: the code pays you to hold capital rather than draw a paycheck.

questions.question: Jordan, 22, earns $45,000 in the 12% bracket. He expects to be in the 24% bracket by age 50. Roth IRA (pay 12% now, withdraw tax-free) or Traditional IRA (deduct 12% now, pay 24% later)?
questions.answer: Roth, paying 12% now beats paying 24% later on the same dollars
choices: Roth, paying 12% now beats paying 24% later on the same dollars
Traditional, the immediate deduction always beats future tax-free growth
Neither, IRAs are only worthwhile for workers earning over $100,000
Both equally, Roth and Traditional always produce the same result
questions.context: The choice is a wager on your future marginal rate. Earn more later: Roth wins. Earn less in retirement: Traditional wins. Most young workers will earn more later, and historic deficits make rates more likely to rise.

questions.question: Tom's 401(k) has a 4-year vesting cliff: leave before year 4 and the employer match goes back to the company. After 3.5 years he's offered a $5,000 raise to switch, but $18,000 of unvested match is on the line. What is the unseen cost?
questions.answer: The forfeited match, the raise must beat what he'd LOSE by leaving early
choices: The forfeited match, the raise must beat what he'd LOSE by leaving early
Nothing, vesting is a formality and bosses always pay the full match
The signing bonus, which is taxed at higher rates than salary
The cost of moving boxes to his new desk on day one
questions.context: Vesting cliffs (typically 3-4 years) are an unseen anti-poaching device. Workers feel the bonus of an outside offer; they often don't compute the forfeited match. The incentive is exactly what the employer designed.

questions.question: Two 25-year-olds buy identical $30,000 cars on 60-month loans. FICO 780 gets 4.5% APR; FICO 620 gets 11% APR. How much MORE does the lower-score buyer pay over 5 years?
questions.answer: About $5,500 more in interest, the score is invisible until the bill arrives
choices: About $5,500 more in interest, the score is invisible until the bill arrives
About $50 more in interest, credit scores barely matter on car loans
Exactly the same, the dealer charges one rate for every buyer
The lower-score buyer pays LESS, banks subsidize poor borrowers
questions.context: FICO ranges 300-850. Every tier costs or saves real money on loans, cards, mortgages, and insurance. Building credit early (pay on time, keep balances low) is a quiet wealth-building skill most kids learn too late.

questions.question: Riley's account has $20. She buys $25 in groceries on her debit card. The bank pays the merchant, charges a $35 overdraft fee, balance is -$40. Why do banks WANT small overdrafts to clear?
questions.answer: $35 on a $5 overdraft is a 700% rate, extraordinarily profitable
choices: $35 on a $5 overdraft is a 700% rate, extraordinarily profitable
Banks lose money on overdrafts but allow them for goodwill
Federal law requires honoring every debit no matter the balance
Banks charge no fees on overdrafts; the $35 is a federal tax
questions.context: Overdraft fees generated $33 billion in US bank revenue in 2019 (CFPB data). The structure targets the smallest balances, the customers least able to pay. The CFPB classified overdraft as high-cost short-term lending.

questions.question: Marcus pulls $40 from an out-of-network ATM: $3.50 to the ATM owner AND $2.50 to his own bank. The $40 cost him $46, almost 15% of the cash. What incentive does this create for banks?
questions.answer: Keep ATM networks fragmented; the customer pays both sides every crossing
choices: Keep ATM networks fragmented; the customer pays both sides every crossing
Build one universal ATM network so anyone can withdraw anywhere free
Eliminate ATMs and force everyone to use mobile banking apps for cash
Subsidize out-of-network use to attract rivals' customers to your bank
questions.context: ATM fees are a classic two-sided market. The home bank charges for using a non-network ATM; the ATM owner charges the customer. Both sides profit when networks stay separate. 'Free ATM nationwide' tiers exist because the fees are non-trivial.

questions.question: Tennessee sales tax is about 9.5% (state + local). A $100 grocery run costs $109.50. The store collects and remits it; the receipt shows the bite. Why is sales tax politically 'easier' than income tax?
questions.answer: The bite spreads across thousands of tiny transactions, painless each
choices: The bite spreads across thousands of tiny transactions, painless each
The state collects from customers directly; the store plays no role
Sales tax funds one program voters approve in a yearly referendum
Sales tax is refunded each April if a year's spend is below a cap
questions.context: Sales tax is a Cantillon-style point-of-transaction levy: visible on each receipt, small enough to ignore. Aggregated, a Tennessee family loses thousands a year. The state pays no enforcement cost; the merchant collects it for them.

questions.question: Social Security FICA stops collecting once a worker's wages cross the annual wage base, $168,600 in 2024. A construction worker earning $50,000 pays 6.2% on every dollar. A surgeon earning $500,000 pays 6.2% only on the first $168,600. What does this design do?
questions.answer: Caps the high earner's contribution, the working-class worker pays a larger SHARE of his wage than the surgeon
choices: Caps the high earner's contribution, the working-class worker pays a larger SHARE of his wage than the surgeon
Forces high earners to pay a higher rate than low earners by progressively scaling the rate past the cap
Has no real effect, the wage base is so high that virtually no working American hits it in practice
Funds Medicare alone, the wage base cap applies only to the 1.45% Medicare portion of FICA
questions.context: The Social Security wage base ratchets up each year. Medicare (1.45%) has NO cap, plus an Additional Medicare Tax (0.9%) above $200K. The structural regressivity of the SS cap is widely noted across the spectrum.

questions.question: In 2024, a single filer in the 22% bracket has bracket lines at $11,600 (10/12%), $47,150 (12/22%), and $100,525 (22/24%). On $60,000 of taxable income, the AVERAGE federal rate is only about 12.4%, even though the top dollar is taxed at 22%. Why?
questions.answer: Each bracket taxes only the SLICE of income inside it; the first $11,600 always pays 10%, no matter what the worker earns above
choices: Each bracket taxes only the SLICE of income inside it; the first $11,600 always pays 10%, no matter what the worker earns above
The IRS averages all brackets together each April and applies one effective rate to the whole annual salary
Workers in the 22% bracket get a special refund that brings their average rate down to 12.4% later in April
The federal government rebates the gap between 22% and 12.4% if total taxable income stays under $75,000
questions.context: Marginal-vs-average is one of the most misunderstood ideas in personal finance. The folk error pushes some workers to refuse raises and overtime, leaving real money on the table.

questions.question: Alex's portfolio is up $5,000 on Apple and down $3,000 on a failed biotech in December. Selling the biotech 'realizes' the loss; selling Apple realizes the gain. Sold together in the same year, his taxable gain becomes only $2,000. What is this called?
questions.answer: Tax-loss harvesting, the code lets losses offset gains, an incentive built into how capital gains work
choices: Tax-loss harvesting, the code lets losses offset gains, an incentive built into how capital gains work
Tax fraud, pairing wins and losses to reduce taxes is illegal under IRS rules in every state
Carryback accounting, losses must be applied to the prior tax year, never the current year
Wash sales, selling at a loss and immediately buying back gives the taxpayer the same deduction
questions.context: Tax-loss harvesting is legal and standard. The wash-sale rule blocks rebuying the SAME security within 30 days; switching to a similar (not identical) holding is allowed. Up to $3,000 of net losses can offset ordinary income annually.

questions.question: Roth IRAs phase out above ~$161,000 single in 2024, high earners can't contribute directly. But they CAN contribute to a Traditional IRA (no income limit) and convert it to Roth the next day. The conversion is taxed but legal. What is this called?
questions.answer: Backdoor Roth, a legal loophole high earners use to access Roth benefits Congress meant to deny them
choices: Backdoor Roth, a legal loophole high earners use to access Roth benefits Congress meant to deny them
Roth bypass, a special IRS program approved annually for retirement savers earning above the cap
Conversion penalty, a fine paid by high earners who try to move money into a Roth account
401(k) substitute, a workplace alternative for executives whose pay exceeds the Roth income limit
questions.context: Congress added the Roth income limit to keep the benefit from high earners. By dropping the income cap on Traditional-to-Roth CONVERSIONS in 2010, they accidentally created the backdoor. Buchanan-Tullock public choice in action.

questions.question: Sarah's job offers a 5% 401(k) match. Salary $60,000, so the match is up to $3,000/year IF she contributes the matching amount. She skips for 30 years, citing tight cash flow. At 7% annual return, what did she give up?
questions.answer: Roughly $300,000, the foregone match plus compounded investment growth over her career
choices: Roughly $300,000, the foregone match plus compounded investment growth over her career
About $90,000, just the cumulative match dollars without any investment growth involved
Only $3,000, the matching contributions roll back to the company at the end of each fiscal year
Nothing meaningful, the employer match is mostly symbolic and rarely worth claiming
questions.context: $3,000/year at 7% over 30 years is about $283,000. The match isn't a bonus; it's compensation the worker chose to leave on the table. Bastiat: what you don't see is often much larger than what you do.

questions.question: Carla quits her $60K marketing job to consult independently at $80K/year. She is thrilled by the 'raise.' At year-end she owes 15.3% self-employment tax ($12,240) plus income tax on the full $80K. She forgot something her W-2 paycheck handled automatically. What?
questions.answer: Quarterly estimated tax payments, the IRS expects 1099 workers to remit four times a year, not just at April
choices: Quarterly estimated tax payments, the IRS expects 1099 workers to remit four times a year, not just at April
An annual professional license fee paid to her state's department of revenue every January 15
A consulting bond required of all 1099 contractors before they can issue invoices to their clients
Sales tax on her services, independent contractors must charge clients state sales tax on each invoice
questions.context: W-2 withholding hides taxes by extracting them every payday. 1099 income arrives gross, so the IRS requires four estimated payments (April, June, September, January). Skip them and underpayment penalties accrue.

questions.question: A 67-year-old retiree wires $250,000 to what he thinks is his daughter's escrow account for a house. The email was a scam, sender address off by one letter. The bank confirms the wire cleared 22 minutes after he sent it. Why is the money likely gone forever?
questions.answer: Wire transfers settle in real time and are final, the receiving bank has already released the funds
choices: Wire transfers settle in real time and are final, the receiving bank has already released the funds
Federal law requires the FBI to refund all wire fraud victims within 90 days of any report
Banks always reverse fraudulent wires on request; the retiree just needs to call the hotline
Wires cannot be sent to scammer accounts because banks screen every transfer for fraud markers
questions.context: Business Email Compromise scams cost US victims $2.9 billion in 2023 (FBI IC3 report). Wires were designed for high-trust commercial settlement, where irreversibility is a feature. Scammers exploit exactly that.

questions.question: Before TCJA 2017, the Smiths itemized: $8,000 state income tax, $6,000 property tax, $4,000 mortgage interest, $2,000 charity = $20,000 deductions, beating the old $12,700 standard. After TCJA capped SALT at $10,000 AND raised the standard to $24,000, what happened?
questions.answer: Standard deduction now beats their itemized total, so they stopped itemizing, which reduced their incentive to donate
choices: Standard deduction now beats their itemized total, so they stopped itemizing, which reduced their incentive to donate
Their tax bill rose $5,000 because TCJA eliminated all itemized deductions for high-property-tax states
They were forced to itemize anyway because their mortgage exceeded the new federal cap on home loans
TCJA had no effect on them; itemizing and the standard deduction produce identical tax results overall
questions.context: TCJA's SALT cap squeezed high-tax-state filers. Post-TCJA, itemized charitable giving dropped because the tax incentive vanished for most. The behavioral response was predictable.

questions.question: Grandpa bought Coca-Cola stock for $1,000 in 1960. It's worth $400,000 when he dies in 2024. His grandson inherits it and sells the next day for $400,000. The realized gain is NOT $399,000. What did the tax code do?
questions.answer: Step-up in basis, the grandson's cost basis resets to date-of-death value, erasing the gain entirely
choices: Step-up in basis, the grandson's cost basis resets to date-of-death value, erasing the gain entirely
Estate tax surcharge, the grandson owes 50% capital gains tax on the entire $399,000 appreciation
Original-basis transfer, the grandson inherits the $1,000 basis and pays full tax on the $399,000 gain
Charity offset, the grandson must donate half the proceeds to avoid all the federal estate taxes
questions.context: Step-up permanently erases unrealized capital gains held until death. The Joint Committee on Taxation estimates ~$40 billion/year in foregone revenue. The break primarily benefits wealthy families and creates a 'lock-in' incentive.

questions.question: Marco has a $5,000 credit card balance at 22% APR. The minimum payment is 2% of balance ($100/month at the start). If he pays only the minimum and never charges another dollar, how long until paid off, and how much interest will he pay?
questions.answer: Over 30 years, paying roughly $9,000 in interest, nearly double the original principal
choices: Over 30 years, paying roughly $9,000 in interest, nearly double the original principal
About 5 years, paying roughly $1,200 in interest, less than the original principal amount
Forever, paying infinite interest, the minimum equals the monthly interest accrual exactly
About 50 months, with virtually no interest, the minimum is far above the daily rate
questions.context: Credit-card minimums are calibrated to extract maximum interest while staying barely above monthly accrual. CARD Act 2009 required statements to show the payoff timeline, but the warning is buried in fine print.

questions.question: A Texas family owns a $300,000 house outright, no mortgage. Annual property tax is $7,500 (Texas averages 1.8-2.5% of assessed value). They could stop paying. What happens if they do for several years running?
questions.answer: The county takes the house, you don't truly own property tax-free; the state is the silent landlord
choices: The county takes the house, you don't truly own property tax-free; the state is the silent landlord
Nothing, Texas has no enforcement mechanism for unpaid property tax on a primary residence ever
The family pays a small late fee and eventually settles when they sell the house years later
Their credit score drops but the house stays in their name forever regardless of unpaid taxes
questions.context: Tax lien foreclosure exists in every US state. Property tax is the closest thing to a true wealth tax: assessed against the asset, not the income, year after year. Ownership is conditional on paying the state its cut.

questions.question: Maria, 45, has $200,000 in a Traditional IRA. In 2024 her income drops to $30,000 because of a sabbatical. Her marginal rate is unusually low (12%). She converts $60,000 of Traditional to Roth, paying $7,200 in tax now. Why might this be brilliant?
questions.answer: She locks in 12% on those dollars; every dollar of future growth comes out tax-free at retirement
choices: She locks in 12% on those dollars; every dollar of future growth comes out tax-free at retirement
She avoids all future required minimum distributions; Roths force withdrawals at age 73 like Traditional IRAs
She doubles her IRA contribution limit for the year; conversions reset the annual cap to zero immediately
She qualifies for extra employer match dollars; conversions trigger an automatic company contribution
questions.context: Roth conversions in a low-income year are among the most tax-efficient moves available. Sabbaticals, early retirement before Social Security, gap years between jobs create one-time low-bracket windows worth exploiting.

questions.question: An American worker earning $50,000 W-2 sees $3,825 (7.65%) withheld for FICA. The employer also remits $3,825. Plus federal income tax (~$4,200) and state tax (~$1,500). Total tax: about $13,350 on what 'costs' her employer $53,825 to hire her. The Tax Foundation puts the US labor wedge near 30%. Who actually 'pays' payroll tax?
questions.answer: Workers bear most of it through lower wages, economists across schools agree the legal 'employer half' is shifted onto the worker invisibly
choices: Workers bear most of it through lower wages, economists across schools agree the legal 'employer half' is shifted onto the worker invisibly
Employers fully absorb their half from corporate profits without any pass-through to workers in any wage form at all
The federal government refunds the employer half each year directly to the worker through scheduled tax credit programs
The wedge is split equally between employer profits, worker wages, and consumer prices in exact proportional thirds always
questions.context: Labor-tax wedge is one of the most-studied results in public finance. Gruber 1997, Saez 2012, OECD comparative data all find workers bear the majority of payroll-tax incidence. Bastiat's seen-vs-unseen at the labor-market level.

questions.question: Survey data from Tax Foundation 2019: roughly 40% of US adults believed 'getting bumped into a higher tax bracket' means the WHOLE salary gets taxed at the higher rate. A nurse offered $5K overtime that would push her last $2K into the 24% bracket calculates: 'I'll lose money.' Why is she wrong, and how much does she actually take home?
questions.answer: Only $2K hits 24%, the rest stays in the 22% bracket; she nets about $3,800 more, just less than the gross $5K
choices: Only $2K hits 24%, the rest stays in the 22% bracket; she nets about $3,800 more, just less than the gross $5K
Her whole salary is reassessed at 24%, so she takes home about $200 LESS than before because of the bracket bump
She owes a one-time bracket penalty of $1,000 to the IRS for crossing the threshold; net loss is $1K total
Her 401(k) match is suspended for the year because high earners lose employer retirement benefits in that bracket
questions.context: The marginal-vs-average misconception has measurable real-world cost. Liebman + Zeckhauser 2004 and behavioral econ literature document workers refusing overtime, raises, and promotions because of this folk error.

questions.question: Mark earns $150K as a software contractor. As a sole proprietor (1099), all $150K is subject to 15.3% SE tax = $22,950. He restructures as an S-corp, pays himself $60K 'reasonable salary' (FICA applies), takes the remaining $90K as a distribution (no FICA). Annual savings: about $13,770. What did the federal code do?
questions.answer: Created an arbitrage opportunity rewarding S-corp formation, Buchanan-Tullock public choice in action; the code shapes the form to extract favorable treatment
choices: Created an arbitrage opportunity rewarding S-corp formation, Buchanan-Tullock public choice in action; the code shapes the form to extract favorable treatment
Eliminated all self-employment tax for high earners by reclassifying their income as a corporate distribution from now on
Forced Mark to incorporate as a C-corp to access lower tax rates the IRS reserves for high-income consultants going forward
Required Mark to pay double FICA on the salary portion to make up for the tax break on his quarterly distributions
questions.context: The 'reasonable salary' standard is loosely enforced; the IRS challenges only egregious cases. Millions of US small businesses operate as S-corps largely for this FICA-arbitrage reason. Incentives shape the form of business.

questions.question: In 2011 Warren Buffett wrote a NYT op-ed: his effective federal tax rate (17.4%) was lower than his secretary's. Why? Most of his income was long-term capital gains and qualified dividends, taxed at 15% (max 20% now). Her income was wages, taxed at marginal 25-28%. Obama proposed the 'Buffett Rule' (min 30% on incomes >$1M); it never passed Congress. What does this illustrate?
questions.answer: The tax code's structural preference for capital over labor, and the political durability of that preference even when major capitalists criticize it openly
choices: The tax code's structural preference for capital over labor, and the political durability of that preference even when major capitalists criticize it openly
A clerical error in Buffett's tax filing that was corrected in 2012 once the IRS audited his returns from the prior decade
The fact that all wages and capital gains are now taxed at identical rates following the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act reforms
The mathematical equivalence between long-term capital gains and ordinary income, Buffett's rate was actually higher than his secretary's
questions.context: Long-term capital gains have been preferentially taxed since 1921 (with brief equalizations 1986-1993). Arguments for: offsets inflation tax of unrealized gains, incentivizes long-term capital. Arguments against: regressive, distorts labor-vs-investment. Bastiat: who lobbies, who pays.

questions.question: Emma puts $6,000 into a Roth IRA at 18 from her camp counselor job. She never contributes another dollar. At 7% over 50 years, the account compounds to roughly $176,000 at 68, tax-free. Her brother, 8 years older, starts at 26 and contributes $6,000 every year for 42 years, ending at roughly $1.4M, also tax-free. What does the math reveal about Emma's choice?
questions.answer: Starting early with even ONE contribution captures decades of compounding the brother's later head start can never replicate dollar-for-dollar
choices: Starting early with even ONE contribution captures decades of compounding the brother's later head start can never replicate dollar-for-dollar
Emma's account is mathematically worthless compared to her brother's; single contributions never compound meaningfully over a half-century
Her brother's larger ending balance proves that delaying retirement saving until career establishment is the optimal strategy for everyone
Roth IRAs only work when funded annually; Emma's account would be reclassified to a Traditional account after 5 years of inactivity
questions.context: Time horizon is the most underappreciated wealth-building variable. Emma's $6K to $176K is a 29x multiple from compounding alone. The brother's $252K of contributions to $1.4M is a 5.5x multiple over a shorter horizon. The earlier the dollar goes in, the more years the curve bends upward.

questions.question: Big-tech firms use 4-year graded vesting (25%/year) or 'cliff' vesting (0% then 100% at year 4). David, 28, joins a startup with 4-year cliff vesting. Annual employer match: $12,000. After 3 years he's offered a job with $10K signing bonus and $20K higher salary. He leaves. What did he forfeit?
questions.answer: $36,000 in unvested match; the signing bonus barely covered one-third of what David walked away from
choices: $36,000 in unvested match; the signing bonus barely covered one-third of what David walked away from
Nothing, federal ERISA law requires immediate 100% vesting of all employer 401(k) contributions for all US workers
The match itself but not the growth; startups must return the principal and let the worker keep gains on it
Only the most recent year's match; vesting cliffs apply only to the contributions made in the final 12 months
questions.context: Cliff vesting is a structural retention tool. The signing bonus often barely offsets the lost match. ERISA (1974) sets maximum vesting schedules (6-year graded, 3-year cliff for most plans), but cliffs are legal and common.

questions.question: A 25-year-old with FICO 680 vs 780 will see different rates over a typical financial life: car loans (~$30K each, every 7 years), credit cards, a mortgage ($300K), insurance premiums. MyFICO estimates a 30-year mortgage rate gap of about 0.7%, roughly $40K interest over the life of one loan. Add all lifetime products. What is the rough cumulative cost of 100 FICO points?
questions.answer: About $100K-$200K over a working life; credit score is one of the largest hidden wealth variables most people never optimize
choices: About $100K-$200K over a working life; credit score is one of the largest hidden wealth variables most people never optimize
Under $5,000 lifetime, FICO scores affect only credit card terms and have minimal real-world impact on overall wealth
Approximately $1 million over a lifetime, even small credit score gaps produce extreme cost differences in every product
Zero meaningful cost, banks and insurers are required by federal law to offer identical rates regardless of credit score
questions.context: FICO is a multiplier on every financial transaction over decades. Insurance, deposits, rates, even apartment rentals all index off it. Score components: payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), history length (15%), credit mix (10%), new credit (10%).

questions.question: TCJA 2017 doubled the standard deduction (single $6,350 to $12,000; married $12,700 to $24,000) AND capped SALT at $10,000. Itemizers dropped from ~30% to ~10% of filers. The share of US households claiming a charitable deduction fell from 25% to 9%. Charitable giving as a share of GDP fell measurably. What does this case demonstrate?
questions.answer: Tax code changes shift real behavior; the charitable-giving incentive vanished for most households and giving fell accordingly
choices: Tax code changes shift real behavior; the charitable-giving incentive vanished for most households and giving fell accordingly
The American people became less generous after 2017 for reasons unrelated to the tax code or rates of itemization
Charitable giving and tax incentives are unrelated; donations are driven purely by social and religious motivations, never tax considerations
TCJA had no effect on charitable behavior because most donors continued to itemize at the same rates as they did before the law
questions.context: Studies after TCJA (Indiana Lilly Family School of Philanthropy 2019; Tax Policy Center 2020) documented the drop. Whether TCJA was good or bad, tax-incentive-driven donations vanished when the incentive vanished. Incentives matter, even for 'altruism.'

questions.question: A working-class family in Tennessee (no state income tax) pays ~9.5% sales tax on purchases. On a $50K budget consuming $40K in taxable goods, that's $3,800 in sales tax. They rent too: the $1,800/month rent embeds the landlord's property tax. Both taxes are invisible at point of payment. Why does this matter for tax policy?
questions.answer: Taxes hidden inside transactions are politically easier to raise than visible income taxes; the bite spreads across thousands of moments, none felt acutely
choices: Taxes hidden inside transactions are politically easier to raise than visible income taxes; the bite spreads across thousands of moments, none felt acutely
Sales and property taxes are deductible against federal income tax, so the family bears no actual burden when filing their annual return in April
Tennessee residents pay the exact same total tax as residents of high-income-tax states like California, just structured differently across categories
Hidden taxes are economically efficient and have no behavioral effect at all on either consumer or producer decisions in the marketplace
questions.context: Sales and property taxes are politically distinct from income tax exactly as Bastiat described: their pain is diffused. Cantillon's 18th-century insight applied to modern taxes: hidden bite stays politically tolerable.

questions.question: Overdraft fees generated about $33 billion in US bank revenue in 2019 (CFPB report). Roughly 8% of customers paid 80% of overdraft fees, disproportionately low-income, often the same households struggling to cover the next bill. Banks could decline transactions when balances are low; instead they 'authorize and charge.' What does this design reveal?
questions.answer: Overdraft fees are a predatory revenue line targeting the most fragile customers; the bank profits exactly when the customer can least afford it
choices: Overdraft fees are a predatory revenue line targeting the most fragile customers; the bank profits exactly when the customer can least afford it
Overdraft fees subsidize free checking accounts for all bank customers, and lower-income customers benefit from the overall arrangement
Banks lose money on overdrafts but allow them to maintain good customer relationships over decades; the fees are charged near cost
Federal regulators require banks to charge overdraft fees on all transactions exceeding the account balance for fraud prevention reasons
questions.context: The 2010 amendment to Regulation E required customer opt-IN for ATM/debit overdraft coverage, but bank defaults are opt-in. Some banks (Capital One 2021, Bank of America 2022) cut or eliminated overdraft fees under public pressure.

questions.question: The OECD's 'tax wedge' = total tax (income + employee FICA + employer FICA) / total labor cost. A US average wage shows ~30%; EU ~42%; Belgium ~53%. Gruber 1997 documented (Chilean data) that most of the employer half shifts onto workers as lower wages. Why does the political distinction matter so little economically?
questions.answer: Statutory incidence is not economic incidence; markets shift burden onto whoever has less elastic supply, almost always the worker, so the 'employer half' is mostly a labeling fiction
choices: Statutory incidence is not economic incidence; markets shift burden onto whoever has less elastic supply, almost always the worker, so the 'employer half' is mostly a labeling fiction
The employer half is genuinely paid by shareholders out of profits, has no effect on wages, and the political split accurately reflects economic reality at every step
Workers bear only the statutory 7.65% and employers truly bear the other half; the OECD measure misleads and overstates the actual tax burden by a wide margin
The wedge falls entirely on consumers as higher prices, so neither workers nor employers pay any portion of the payroll tax at market equilibrium under standard assumptions
questions.context: Public-finance economics distinguishes legal incidence (who writes the check) from economic incidence (who bears the cost). Across Gruber 1997, Saez 2012, Bozio et al. 2017, and OECD's own work, workers bear most of the wedge through lower wages. The 50/50 split is political fiction.

questions.question: The marginal-vs-average confusion isn't trivial. Studies (Liebman + Zeckhauser 2004; Rees-Jones + Taubinsky 2020) document workers refusing raises, declining overtime, leaving 401(k) match unclaimed, structuring side-gig hours to stay 'under' bracket lines they don't actually fear. Behavioral public finance estimates the misperception costs workers tens of billions annually. What does this reveal about complexity?
questions.answer: Complexity has a real cost; it produces decisions worse than a simpler code by mis-shaping the choices citizens make about their own labor
choices: Complexity has a real cost; it produces decisions worse than a simpler code by mis-shaping the choices citizens make about their own labor
Tax-code complexity is harmless to most workers because automatic withholding handles everything via the employer's payroll systems automatically
Voters consistently understand marginal-vs-average in survey data, and the studies cited were methodologically flawed and have since been retracted
Behavioral economics has shown the marginal-vs-average misconception improves household decision-making by encouraging the conservative choices people should make
questions.context: Complexity-tax is itself a Bastiat unseen cost. Seen: 70,000 pages of IRS code, $40B/year in compliance, H&R Block + TurboTax franchises. Unseen: worse-than-optimal labor-market decisions by millions who can't decode the system. Friedman, Sowell, Caplan, Murphy converge here.

questions.question: Long-term capital gains have been preferentially taxed since 1921. Combined with step-up basis at death and carried-interest treatment, investors hold appreciated assets longer than optimal to defer or erase tax, the 'lock-in effect.' JCT puts step-up alone near $40B/year. Gordon and Slemrod argue the system distorts portfolio rebalancing. What does Bastiat reveal?
questions.answer: Seen: lower capital gains revenue. Unseen: capital trapped in legacy positions instead of flowing to its highest-value use, dynamism foregone
choices: Seen: lower capital gains revenue. Unseen: capital trapped in legacy positions instead of flowing to its highest-value use, dynamism foregone
Capital gains preferences are economically neutral; investors always rebalance optimally regardless of tax, and Gordon and Slemrod decisively refuted lock-in
The system perfectly aligns investor and society interest by rewarding patience and discouraging destabilizing short-term trading, no economic cost at all
Step-up basis was repealed in 2010 with the estate tax; the lock-in distortion no longer exists in the current federal system and citations to it are dated
questions.context: Lock-in is one of the cleanest cases where tax policy produces measurable misallocation. Revenue numbers tell only the seen side; the unseen (capital frozen in legacy holdings, suboptimal portfolios, reduced dynamism) is larger. Reform proposals exist but the political case keeping the preference is a Buchanan-Tullock pattern.

questions.question: Roth-vs-Traditional is a wager on future tax rates. As of 2024: US federal debt-to-GDP near 124% (highest since 1946). Social Security trust fund projected exhausted ~2033. Demographics: working-age per retiree falling from 5:1 (1960) to ~2.1:1 (2030s). What does that imply for someone choosing now?
questions.answer: Future US tax rates are more likely to rise than fall; Roth (pay now at the known rate) hedges against the higher rates demographic and fiscal pressure make probable
choices: Future US tax rates are more likely to rise than fall; Roth (pay now at the known rate) hedges against the higher rates demographic and fiscal pressure make probable
Future US tax rates will certainly fall because productivity growth will outpace fiscal pressure and cut federal revenue needs to a fraction of today's
Future rates are random and unknowable, so the Roth-vs-Traditional choice should be made by coin flip; no rational analysis is possible at all
MMT proves the federal government can fund any deficit without raising taxes ever again, so Roth and Traditional produce identical after-tax results long-run
questions.context: Roth-vs-Traditional is genuinely uncertain, the future is. But it isn't random. US fiscal trajectory creates real political pressure for higher future taxes on retirement income. The Austrian point: governments can debase, raise rates, or cut benefits, but the gap must close.

questions.question: The 1978 Revenue Act IRC 401(k) was a minor provision letting executives defer bonuses tax-free. Ted Benna, a benefits consultant, in 1980 interpreted it as a vehicle for all employees with employer matching, and the modern 401(k) was born. Shifting from defined-benefit pensions (employer bears risk) to 401(k)s (worker bears it) has been the largest US retirement-policy change in 50 years. Who benefited?
questions.answer: Employers shed pension liability and market risk; workers gained portability but lost guaranteed benefits; both sides benefit vs alternatives, with the worker now bearing risks the employer used to
choices: Employers shed pension liability and market risk; workers gained portability but lost guaranteed benefits; both sides benefit vs alternatives, with the worker now bearing risks the employer used to
Only employers benefited; workers received no advantages whatsoever, and the change was a unilateral wage cut imposed by management across all US industries
Only workers benefited; 401(k)s pay strictly higher returns than pensions, and matching contributions exceed what pension benefits would have paid over a career
Neither benefited; the shift was federal regulatory mandate with no economic logic on either side, and US retirement security has measurably fallen since 1980 because of it
questions.context: Defined-benefit pensions put longevity + investment risk on the employer. Defined-contribution plans shift both to the worker. The employer match is partial compensation for assuming risks the employer used to bear. ERISA (1974), IRC 401(k), and the slow pension freeze through the 80s-2000s shape the modern retirement landscape.

questions.question: Until the late 1970s, most US states had usury laws capping consumer loans around 18%. In 1978 the Supreme Court ruled in Marquette National Bank v. First of Omaha that an issuer could 'export' its HOME state's rate, letting banks relocate to Delaware and South Dakota with no caps. Within a decade, US card rates rose from ~12% to 18-22%+. What does this illustrate?
questions.answer: Federal preemption + interstate banking dismantled state-level interest caps; political choice, not 'market evolution,' produced the modern credit-card APR landscape
choices: Federal preemption + interstate banking dismantled state-level interest caps; political choice, not 'market evolution,' produced the modern credit-card APR landscape
Free-market competition naturally produced higher card rates because consumers preferred to pay much more for the convenience of charging purchases at stores
Marquette was reversed by the Truth in Lending Act of 1968, fully restoring state usury caps that remain in effect across all 50 states without exception
Card APRs are set directly by the Federal Reserve in monthly meetings, with no connection to state usury law, Marquette, or any 1970s court ruling about credit
questions.context: Marquette is foundational in modern US consumer-credit history. South Dakota then Delaware moved aggressively to attract bank charters by removing usury caps. The resulting industry (22-29% APRs, minimum-payment math optimized for revenue) emerged from one Supreme Court ruling plus state-level rate competition.

questions.question: TCJA 2017 raised the standard deduction (single $6,350 to $12,000; married $12,700 to $24,000), capped SALT at $10,000, and reduced AMT scope. Itemizers dropped from ~30% to ~10%. Charitable giving as share of GDP fell from ~2.1% to ~1.9% within 2 years. Indiana Lilly estimated $16-20B/year in foregone giving. Bastiat read?
questions.answer: Seen: a simpler tax code. Unseen: billions in foregone charitable transfers responding to a tax incentive, donations that would have flowed to civil society now didn't
choices: Seen: a simpler tax code. Unseen: billions in foregone charitable transfers responding to a tax incentive, donations that would have flowed to civil society now didn't
TCJA had no impact on charitable giving; the Indiana Lilly studies were retracted in 2020 after critics found methodological errors in the donation projections
Seen: higher federal revenue. Unseen: political mobilization of charities against future reform; the law produced no measurable change in actual donation behavior
Charitable giving rose after TCJA because the doubled standard deduction freed up household cash that previously went to tax payments under the older code
questions.context: Reasonable people disagree on TCJA's net effect. The Bastiat point is methodological: tax-code changes have visible effects (federal revenue, top marginal rates) and invisible effects (foregone behavior the prior code had incentivized). Charitable incentives ARE incentives; remove them, behavior responds.

questions.question: American homeowners pay property tax annually on assessed value. NJ averages ~2.2%; Texas similar. On a $400K home that's $8,800/year; over 30 years with reassessments, over $300K. A homeowner who 'owns outright' pays the state more, total, than they paid for the house. If you stop paying, the state takes the property. What does this reveal?
questions.answer: Property tax is the closest thing to a true wealth tax in the US; the state is the silent senior landlord, 'ownership' is conditional on annual payment in perpetuity
choices: Property tax is the closest thing to a true wealth tax in the US; the state is the silent senior landlord, 'ownership' is conditional on annual payment in perpetuity
Property tax is voluntary in most states; homeowners can opt out by registering the property as a private trust under federal common-law homestead protections
Property tax is a fair user fee for local services like schools and roads, with no wealth-tax character and no behavioral or distributional consequence in any state
Property tax was effectively eliminated after California's Proposition 13 in 1978; only a few coastal states still levy it on residential property under federal grandfathering
questions.context: Property tax has a particular Bastiat character: visible (most people know they pay it) yet psychologically invisible (assessed via bills, escrow, mortgage statements). State authority over the property is permanent and conditional on payment; the 'ownership' label is partly misleading.

questions.question: Business email compromise (BEC) scams cost US victims $2.9B in 2023 (FBI IC3 report). Typical attack: scammer spoofs a vendor email, victim wires to a fake account, the wire clears within hours. Recovery: under 10%. Wire fees of $25-50 reflect same-day settlement, no reversibility. Bitcoin shares the property: a confirmed transaction is final. LESSON?
questions.answer: Irreversibility is a feature, not a bug; it makes settlement final but the user bears the cost of mistakes, the trade-off applies to wires AND Bitcoin AND every settled-money system
choices: Irreversibility is a feature, not a bug; it makes settlement final but the user bears the cost of mistakes, the trade-off applies to wires AND Bitcoin AND every settled-money system
Wire transfers and Bitcoin are economically identical; both are fully reversible if requested through the proper bank channel or any major Bitcoin wallet's support
Federal law requires both wires and Bitcoin to be reversible within 60 days for fraud claims, so the IC3 figures are overstated by at least an order of magnitude
Only Bitcoin is technically irreversible; bank wires can always be cancelled within minutes if the sender simply calls the originating bank's customer service line
questions.context: Settlement finality is one of money's least-discussed but most-important properties. Gold coins handed over, paper notes, wire transfers, and Bitcoin all share it. Credit cards and ACH built reversibility on top of settlement; that reversibility costs money. Knowing which trade your transaction made is a citizenship skill.

questions.question: An American family earning $80K in 2024 faces: federal income tax (~10% effective, 22% marginal), employee FICA (7.65%) + employer FICA (7.65%, shifted onto wages), state income tax (0-13%), state sales tax (~7%), property tax embedded in rent (1-2%), gas tax, excise taxes, compliance costs. The Tax Foundation puts total federal+state+local on median households at 25-35% of all activity. What does Bastiat reveal?
questions.answer: Each tax LOOKS modest; the cumulative wedge is the largest single cost the household never directly sees, seen-vs-unseen repeated at every layer until it adds up to a third of life's activity
choices: Each tax LOOKS modest; the cumulative wedge is the largest single cost the household never directly sees, seen-vs-unseen repeated at every layer until it adds up to a third of life's activity
Total tax burden on US households is roughly 5-8% of spending, a small fraction that has only minimal effect on standard of living in any income bracket
Households pay essentially no real tax because federal benefits (Social Security, Medicare, public schools) exceed tax payments, so net transfer is positive in every bracket
Incidence falls entirely on corporations and high earners; median households pay zero net federal tax once credits and deductions are properly applied at filing
questions.context: Compound-tax wedge is among the cleanest applications of Bastiat's method. No single tax feels overwhelming; the aggregate is 25-35% of economic activity, sustained by a code so complex no citizen can track it. The Austrian + public-choice tradition has argued for decades this complexity serves the political-economic incentives of those writing the code.
